section.title: Diotrephes Rebuked
section.sectionRationale: The letter's dark centre: a church leader named Diotrephes, who loves to be first, rejects the elder's authority, slanders him, refuses the travelling brothers, and expels those who would welcome them. The elder answers with a plain principle: do not imitate evil but good.
section.thesis: Self-exalting leadership that loves preeminence stands opposed to the truth, and the way forward is not to copy such evil but to imitate what is good, for the one who does good is of God.
section.frameNote: Two beats: the charge against Diotrephes, who loves to be first; and the elder's appeal to imitate good rather than evil.

units.label: The charge against Diotrephes
units.note: a man who loves to be first

verses.text: I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who {{philoproteuo|loves to be first}}, will not accept our instruction.

So if I come, I will call attention to his {{phlyareo|malicious slander}} against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.

units.label: The appeal to imitate good
units.note: the one who does good is of God

verses.text: Beloved, do not {{mimeomai|imitate}} what is evil, but what is good. The one who {{agathopoieo|does good}} is of God; the one who {{kakopoieo|does evil}} has not seen God.

philoproteuo.gloss: To love to be first, to crave preeminence and the top place. It appears only here in the New Testament, coined to expose Diotrephes exactly. His root sin is not false doctrine but a hunger for personal supremacy that poisons everything he does in the church.

phlyareo.gloss: To talk nonsense against, to bring unjustified and malicious charges. It pictures empty, wicked words used as weapons. Diotrephes did not refute the elder with truth; he tore at him with baseless slander, the tool of a man defending his own position.

mimeomai.gloss: To imitate, to copy as a pattern; the root of the word mimic. Discipleship works by imitation, so the elder tells Gaius which pattern to follow: not the evil of Diotrephes but the good, which ultimately means following God and those who reflect Him.

agathopoieo.gloss: To do good, to act rightly and beneficially. The one who habitually does good shows that he belongs to God, is of God, sharing His character. Doing good here is the visible evidence of a life truly connected to God.

kakopoieo.gloss: To do evil, to act wickedly. The one whose settled practice is evil, like Diotrephes, shows he has not seen God, has no real knowledge of or fellowship with Him. Conduct reveals the heart: what we habitually do exposes whose we are.

basic.context: Now the tone darkens. A man named Diotrephes had taken charge in a church and loved being first. He rejected the elder's authority, spread malicious lies about him, refused to welcome the travelling gospel workers, and even threw out members who did welcome them. The elder says he will deal with this if he comes, and then gives Gaius a simple rule: do not copy evil, copy good.
basic.hermeneutics: This describes a real and ugly church conflict; it does not commend Diotrephes. The lasting lessons are sharp: leadership that craves being first is a serious danger, slander and shutting people out are marks of a heart far from God, and the test of anyone's claim to know God is whether they actually do good.
basic.originalLanguages: Diotrephes is defined by a rare word, philoproteuo, loves to be first. He attacks the elder with phlyareo, malicious empty talk, slander. The elder tells Gaius to mimeomai, imitate, not evil but good. The one who does good, agathopoieo, is of God; the one who does evil, kakopoieo, has not seen God.
basic.typology: Diotrephes, grasping to be first, is the opposite of Christ, who did not grasp at status but made Himself nothing and took the lowest place to serve. He is a warning picture of the self-exalting leader, set against Jesus, the servant King who is truly first because He humbled Himself.
basic.christ: Jesus taught that whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all, and He lived it, washing His disciples' feet and dying for them. Diotrephes is everything Christ is not. To imitate what is good is to imitate Christ, the one who did good and is of God in the fullest sense.
basic.god: God is dishonoured by proud, domineering leadership that loves the top place and shuts others out. He is honoured by humble service and by doing good. And He sees the heart: our habits of good or evil reveal whether we truly know Him.
basic.crossReferences: Jesus says the greatest must be the servant. Paul says Christ did not grasp at equality but humbled Himself. And Peter warns elders not to lord it over the flock but to be examples to it.
basic.oneStory: The Bible's story is the undoing of proud self-rule by the humble Servant King. Diotrephes shows the old grasping way still at work inside the church, while Christ shows the new way of lowly service. Gaius, and every believer, is called to imitate the good and so belong to God.

context.literary:
The letter turns sharply at verse 9. Verses 5 to 8 were about a man who opened his door; verses 9 and 10 are about a man who shut one. The two are placed side by side on purpose. The same activity, how a church treats the brothers, is described twice, first in a believer who welcomes and then in a leader who refuses. The contrast does the teaching without needing a lecture.

The description of Diotrephes is built in layers. First comes the root, that he loves to be first, which is a heart condition. Then come the acts that grow from it, listed in a rising series: he does not accept the elder's word, he spreads false and malicious talk, he refuses the brothers, he stops others who want to receive them, and he expels those who do. Each step goes further than the last, and the final one turns private pride into public harm.

The elder's own response is measured. He mentions a letter already written, a promise to come and deal with the matter, and then, in verse 11, a turn to the reader. The shift from the third person to a direct address to Gaius is important. The elder does not ask Gaius to confront Diotrephes publicly, as far as the text says. He asks him to choose which example to follow.

Verse 11 is a hinge. It is a general maxim, in two balanced halves, "the one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God." The phrase is generalised from Diotrephes and prepares for Demetrius in verse 12, who will serve as the good example. The three men, Gaius, Diotrephes and Demetrius, form a triptych, and verse 11 is the frame that tells us how to look at it.
context.historical:
Churches in the first century met mostly in homes, and a church's life depended on whoever owned or ran the house. A person with space, money and standing could easily become the leader without any formal appointment, and the elders appointed by the apostles, Acts 14:23, did not always keep authority in the right hands. Diotrephes is a case of a man who has seized the place of leader and will not share it.

The elder describes him as unwilling to "accept" what comes from the elder's side. The same Greek verb for refusing appears twice, once of the elder's message and once of the brothers, so Diotrephes' refusal of the travellers is bound up with a refusal of the elder. It is likely that he saw the travelling workers as a threat to his control, because they carried the elder's authority and reported to a wider network. Pushing them out also cut off the lines of correction.

The elder mentions that he has already written to the church. This letter has not survived. It may have been a short note that Diotrephes suppressed, and some have suggested it was 2 John, though most think it was a lost letter. In either case, the writer's earlier appeal had failed.

The act of putting people out of the church was serious. In a small community where table fellowship, patronage and worship were bound together, expulsion cut a believer from friends, support and identity. Jesus Himself had warned that his followers would be thrown out of the synagogue, John 16:2, and the verb used in 3 John 10 is the same one used for the man born blind, John 9:34. For a leader to use the same weapon against hospitable believers was a reversal of its proper purpose.
context.canonical:
The love of first place is an old problem among God's people. Moses faced it in Korah's rebellion, Numbers 16:3. Disciples argued about it at the last supper, Luke 22:24, and Jesus answered by turning the idea of greatness upside down: the one who leads is to serve, Luke 22:26, and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all, Mark 10:44. Paul told the Philippians to do nothing from selfish ambition, Philippians 2:3, and set Christ before them as the pattern, Philippians 2:6-8.

The New Testament also records leaders who hurt the church from within. Paul warned the Ephesian elders that men would arise from their own number to draw away disciples, Acts 20:29-30. Peter told elders not to lord it over those in their care but to be examples, 1 Peter 5:3. Jesus Himself rebuked the rulers of the Gentiles who lord it over others, and said it must not be so among His people, Mark 10:42-43.

Verse 11 has a close companion in 1 John 3:6-10, where the one who practises righteousness is righteous and the one who does not is not of God, and in John 3:21, where the one who practises truth comes to the light. First John also reverses the idea of seeing God: whoever continues to sin has not seen or known Him, 1 John 3:6, and whoever hates his brother cannot love God whom he has not seen, 1 John 4:20.

The call to imitate good has a long history too. Paul urges imitation of himself as he imitates Christ, 1 Corinthians 11:1, and Hebrews bids believers remember their leaders and imitate their faith, Hebrews 13:7. The command is always to imitate what truly follows Christ.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The elder wants Gaius to know the facts and to be ready to act on them. He names Diotrephes plainly, not leaving the matter in generalities, because Gaius cannot stand against a problem he does not understand. He lists the offences so that Gaius will not mistake them for a matter of style or personality.

He also wants Gaius to stay on the right side of the matter without becoming like the man he opposes. The command of verse 11, not to imitate evil but good, speaks to this danger. A person standing against a bully is tempted to respond with the same bullying. The elder offers a different resolve: keep doing good, keep welcoming the brothers and let the pattern speak.

Verse 10 shows that the elder intends to come and act. This is not an idle threat but a statement of apostolic responsibility. Yet his words to Gaius are mostly about Gaius. The first hearers would have understood that the elder's authority was not at stake in a personal sense: what was at stake was whether a church would keep its doors open to Christ's messengers. The elder wants Gaius to hear the matter as a test of character, and to be sure of who belongs to God by the fruit of what they do.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This passage records a real dispute and the elder's description of one man's conduct. It does not command us to treat every strong leader as a Diotrephes or to expel anyone who disagrees. It does not tell us exactly how to handle a church leader who refuses accountability, though it shows that the elder planned to confront him in person and in public.

What it prescribes is plain at its centre. Do not imitate what is evil, and do imitate what is good. The marks of Diotrephes, love of first place, slander, shutting out genuine believers and punishing those who welcome them, are warning signs to be recognised and avoided in ourselves as well as in others. The passage also gives a test, that doing good shows a person is of God, which should be applied with humility and not as a weapon. A church that sees these signs in its leadership should address them honestly, and any one of us should ask whether our own habits are drawing people in or keeping them out.

debates.question: What was Diotrephes' fault: bad doctrine or bad character?

views.label: Mainly pride and the love of control
views.case: The elder lists no false teaching. He lists pride, slander and exclusion, and he says Diotrephes loves to be first. Most readers conclude that the problem is personal ambition and the refusal of accountability, which is a moral and relational failure.

views.label: Doctrinal error underlies it
views.case: Some have suggested that Diotrephes' refusal of the elder's authority was linked to a different teaching, perhaps a rival view of leadership or of the elder's circle of churches. The letter does not say this, but the elder's closeness to a 2 John that guards against false teachers is sometimes taken to imply it.

views.label: A conflict of authority between local and wider leadership
views.case: Others see a clash between a local leader who wanted autonomy and an apostolic circle that expected the churches to receive its delegates. On this reading the matter is about structure, with Diotrephes defending his territory.

debates.bearing: The text itself supports the first view most directly. Whatever else lay behind it, the elder judges the conduct, and he judges it by a moral measure: the one who does evil has not seen God.

debates.question: What was the earlier letter the elder had written to the church?

views.label: A lost letter
views.case: Most scholars hold that the elder wrote a short letter, now lost, asking the church to receive his delegates. The wording of verse 9 is that he wrote 'something' to the church, and nothing in the surviving letters matches it closely enough to be certain. The New Testament includes only a small fraction of what the apostles wrote.

views.label: Second John
views.case: Some suggest the earlier letter was 2 John, which is addressed to a church, shows the elder's concern with welcome and refusal, and might have been suppressed by Diotrephes. Others reply that 2 John is about false teachers and does not fit a request to receive friendly missionaries.

views.label: Left open
views.case: The elder says only that he wrote something to the church. Since the wording gives no title, length or subject beyond the matter at hand, a careful reader can say that the letter existed and was ignored, and leave its identity unsettled.

debates.bearing: The identity does not change the lesson. What matters is that the elder had already appealed through the proper channel and been refused, so his planned visit is a reasonable next step and not a hasty one.

study.originalLanguages:
The man is defined by a compound found only here in the New Testament, philoproteuo, built from phileo, "to love," and a stem for "first place." The root of the second half, proteuo, appears elsewhere only in Colossians 1:18, of Christ, who is to have "preeminence" in all things. That is a pointed irony: the one person to whom first place belongs, Christ, is the one Diotrephes pushes aside by taking it for himself. The present participle presents it as a settled disposition, not a single act.

His refusal is expressed with epidechomai, "to receive, to welcome." The elder says Diotrephes does not receive "us," and then, in verse 10, that he does not receive "the brothers." The English text renders the first as accepting instruction and the second as welcoming, which hides the fact that the same verb is used twice. The effect in Greek is a chain: he will not welcome the elder, therefore he will not welcome the elder's people. The way to read the passage is to see that rejecting authority and rejecting the brothers are the same act.

The "malicious slander" is phlyareo, a verb used only here in the New Testament, meaning to talk nonsense or spout empty words, and here to do so against someone. A related adjective in 1 Timothy 5:13 describes idle gossips. The elder's addition of "evil" words makes it more than idle chat: it is talk that harms. The verb for "call attention to" in verse 10 means to remind or recall, so the elder will bring Diotrephes' own deeds to mind when he comes.

The last charge is that he "puts out" those who want to welcome, using ekballo, to throw out. It is the same verb used when the religious leaders drove out the man born blind, John 9:34. The present tense may describe either repeated action or an ongoing practice.

In verse 11 the command is mimeomai in the present imperative, "stop imitating" or "do not make a habit of imitating." The same stem gives us mimic. Paul uses it of imitating himself, 2 Thessalonians 3:7, and Hebrews uses it of imitating faith, Hebrews 13:7. The contrasting verbs agathopoieo and kakopoieo, "to do good" and "to do evil," appear in Luke 6:9 and 1 Peter 2:15, and the perfect tense of "has seen" in the final clause points to a settled state: such a person has not come to see God, and remains in that condition.

typology.type: Diotrephes, the one who loves to be first
typology.fulfillment: Diotrephes is the opposite of Christ, who, 'existing in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be grasped,' but humbled Himself, Philippians 2:6-8. He also recalls Satan's proud grasping in Isaiah 14:13-14, and the old desire of humans to be like God, Genesis 3:5. The escalation is that Christ is truly first, Colossians 1:18, and receives the place by giving Himself away. The type is negative and falls short in that Diotrephes is a warning, not a picture of redemption.

Those who are thrown out for welcoming the brothers share the lot of the man born blind, who was thrown out for confessing Christ, John 9:34, and of Christ Himself, who was cast out of the city, Luke 4:29, and suffered outside the gate, Hebrews 13:12-13. The escalation is that Christ bears the exclusion fully and then opens the door for all who come to Him. The correspondence falls short because the expelled in this letter are ordinary believers and not saviours.

typology.type: Imitating the good, the one who does good is of God
typology.fulfillment: The pattern for imitation is Jesus, who 'went around doing good,' Acts 10:38, and left an example so that we should follow in His steps, 1 Peter 2:21. The escalation is that believers do not only copy a good example but are united to Him and renewed by His Spirit, Ephesians 5:1-2. The type falls short because human examples such as Gaius are imperfect, and imitation is always an imitation of Christ in them, 1 Corinthians 11:1.

study.christ:
Diotrephes is best understood by contrast with Christ. The letter does not mention Jesus, but every phrase about Diotrephes invites the comparison. He loves to be first, while Christ "did not consider equality with God something to be grasped," and made Himself nothing, Philippians 2:6-7. He refuses to receive the brothers, while Christ received sinners and ate with them, Luke 15:2. He drives people out of the church, while Christ said, "whoever comes to Me I will never drive away," John 6:37. He uses power for himself, while Christ washed His disciples' feet, John 13:14-15, and gave His life as a ransom for many, Mark 10:45.

The passage also touches the deepest claim about Christ's place. Paul says that Christ is the head of the body and that in all things He is to have preeminence, Colossians 1:18. The verb behind that word is the root of the one used of Diotrephes. This does not make Diotrephes a rival to Christ in any literal way, but it shows what he does: he sits in a seat that belongs to the Lord. Every church leader is a steward and a servant, never the head. The right to be first has been won by the One who died, and it is exercised in service.

Verse 11 gives a standard that is fulfilled in Him. The one who does good is of God. Jesus is the one who went about doing good, Acts 10:38, and who is the way to see God. "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father," John 14:9. The elder's phrase "has not seen God" in the second half of the verse is thus a statement about people who stay far from Christ, since in Him God has been seen, John 1:18.

There is a warning against forced allegory here. Gaius is not Christ and Diotrephes is not the devil in disguise. But the pattern is real: a servant King and a would-be ruler of the church. When the Lord's people have to choose whom to follow, the choice is between the way of Diotrephes and the way of the One who laid down His life for the sheep, John 10:11.
study.god:
This passage reveals a God who judges the heart through its fruit. The elder does not say that the one who does good earns God, but that such a person is "of God," belonging to Him by birth and showing the family likeness. The one who does evil has not seen Him. God is known by those who share His character, and no claim to know Him survives a life that contradicts it, as 1 John 3:10 and 4:20 also teach.

It also shows that God opposes pride. The elder sets Diotrephes' love of first place against the humility of Christ, and the rest of Scripture is plain about God's attitude: He resists the proud and gives grace to the humble, James 4:6 and 1 Peter 5:5. The same God who exalts the humble will bring down the ones who exalt themselves, Luke 14:11. The danger of religious leadership is greater than most, because the leader speaks in God's name, and the elder's severity reflects that.

Third, the passage shows a God who is faithful to His messengers. The brothers who are turned away have not been forgotten. God sees the exclusion and stands behind those who go out for the Name. He is also a God who works by accountability, since the elder will come and deal with the matter, and He has set apostles and elders to guard His people.

A tension is held here as well. God allows a man like Diotrephes to hold a place in His church, to speak against His apostle and to hurt believers, and does not at once remove him. The letter does not explain why. It offers no sentimental answer. It shows God's patience alongside the clear promise of correction, and it leaves Gaius with a command: do good.

For worship, the passage asks us to see leadership as a trust and not a prize, and to honour God by treating His people as the household He loves. When we welcome those the world pushes away, we are acting in line with His character, and we are His children by the same fruit.

crossReferences.note: Jesus says that those the Gentiles consider rulers lord it over them, but it is not to be so among His people. Whoever wants to be first must be the slave of all, for the Son of Man came to serve. This is the direct answer to Diotrephes' love of first place.

Paul asks believers to do nothing from selfish ambition and holds up Christ, who did not grasp at equality with God but took the form of a servant. The passage is the positive picture set against the negative picture of Diotrephes.
Elders are to shepherd willingly and not lord it over those entrusted to them but to be examples to the flock. The standard Peter sets for elders is the standard Diotrephes breaks.

Paul warns the Ephesian elders that from their own number men will rise up to draw disciples after themselves. It shows that harm from inside the leadership was expected, and that Diotrephes was not an unprecedented case.

Practising righteousness or sin shows who is a child of God and who is not. Verse 10 says that anyone who does not practise righteousness is not of God. The test the elder applies in verse 11 is the same test, in the same words.

The leaders threw out the man born blind after he confessed Jesus. It uses the same verb as the elder uses of Diotrephes, and it shows the pattern of those in power casting out the ones who side with Christ.

Christ is the head of the body and in everything is to have the first place. The word for preeminence is related to the verb at the root of Diotrephes' name for himself, and shows whose place he is trying to take.

At the last supper the disciples argue about who is the greatest, and Jesus says that the greatest should be as the one who serves, pointing to Himself as one who serves. The love of first place was a standing temptation even for the Twelve.

Paul tells the Corinthians to imitate him as he imitates Christ. It gives the proper meaning of imitation in verse 11: following leaders only as far as they follow Christ, and being willing to be copied for that reason.

Anyone who says he loves God but hates his brother is a liar, because he cannot love God whom he has not seen. It develops the idea of seeing God in the elder's last clause, tying knowledge of God to love of the brothers.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a creature who wanted to be like God, Genesis 3:5, and the same impulse runs through it: Cain, the builders of Babel, Korah, Absalom and the kings who made themselves great at the expense of their people. Against this stands God's own way of rule, which is shepherding. He is the shepherd of Israel, Psalm 80:1, and the prophets condemn the shepherds who feed themselves and not the flock, Ezekiel 34:2-4. The failure of leaders to care for those in their charge is one of the long sorrows of the Old Testament, and the promise is that God will come Himself and be the shepherd, Ezekiel 34:11-16.

That promise is kept in Christ, the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. He establishes a new kind of leadership, in which the greatest serves, and He sends out under-shepherds to follow Him, John 21:15-17. The early churches are the first tests of this new way. Some elders are humble and faithful, and some, like Diotrephes, take the old way of self-promotion into the new community. The New Testament does not conceal this. It shows that the church lives with the same struggle against pride that the whole Bible records.

Third John gives one of its sharpest portraits. A man who loves to be first sits inside the church, shutting out the very people sent for the gospel. The old story of grasping, which began in the garden, has come into the house of God. The answer is the same one the Bible has always given: the humble will be exalted and the proud will be brought low, and those who belong to God will do good.

The story ends with all false rule removed. In the new creation there is one throne and one Lamb, and those who serve Him will reign, Revelation 22:3-5. No one there will love to be first, because the first place is held by the One who gave it away for others. Until then, the church must read this brief and painful portrait and keep watching for the old pride in its own ranks, and choose, with Gaius, to imitate what is good.

sermon.title: The Condemnation of Diotrephes
sermon.why: Begg devotes this message in his 3 John series to Diotrephes, showing how a bad ego left unchecked produces chaos in the church, and setting his self-exaltation against the call to imitate what is good. A clear, orthodox treatment of this movement.

quiz.q: What was the root problem with Diotrephes?

options.text: He loved to be first, craving preeminence and rejecting others' authority.
options.note: Verse 9 names his love of being first as the driving sin behind his behaviour.

options.text: He abused his authority, rejecting oversight and controlling the church.
options.note: True of his conduct, but Scripture roots it in his love of being first.
The text never charges him with false teaching; the issue is pride and power.

options.text: He was simply shy and withdrawn.
options.note: He was domineering and aggressive, not withdrawn.

quiz.q: What did Diotrephes do to those who wanted to welcome the brothers?

options.text: He forbade them and even put them out of the church.
options.note: Verse 10 records that he expelled those who welcomed the workers.

options.text: He refused to welcome the brothers and pressured others to do the same.
options.note: True, but the sharpest detail is that he expelled those who did welcome them.

options.text: He quietly disagreed but let them carry on.
options.note: He did not merely disagree; he actively forbade and expelled them.

options.text: He welcomed the brothers himself instead.
options.note: He refused to welcome them at all.

quiz.q: What principle does the elder give Gaius in verse 11?

options.text: Do not imitate evil but good, for the one who does good is of God.
options.note: Verse 11 sets the governing rule: copy good, not evil, as the mark of belonging to God.

options.text: Copy good examples rather than bad ones in the church.
options.note: Right as far as it goes, but it omits the test that doing good shows we are of God.

options.text: Avoid all church leaders from now on.
options.note: The point is discernment between good and evil, not withdrawal from the church.

options.text: Repay Diotrephes with the same slander.
options.note: The call is to imitate good, not to answer evil with evil.

quiz.q: How does Diotrephes contrast with Jesus?

options.text: Diotrephes grasped to be first; Jesus took the servant's place and made Himself last.
options.note: Christ, who served and washed feet, is the opposite of Diotrephes, Mark 10:45.

options.text: Jesus served others, while Diotrephes served only himself.
options.note: True and to the point, a simpler statement of the same contrast.

options.text: Both simply wanted to lead the church well.
options.note: Diotrephes wanted supremacy for himself; Jesus led by humble service.

options.text: Diotrephes is a good model of leadership to follow.
options.note: He is a warning, the very opposite of Christlike leadership.

questions: Diotrephes loved to be first. Where do you notice the desire to be first, to be seen, or to be in control creeping into your own heart?
He used slander to protect his position. When you feel threatened, do you reach for truth and humility, or for words that tear others down?
The elder tells Gaius to imitate good, not evil. Whose life are you actually copying, and is it drawing you toward Christ or away from Him?
Doing good is the evidence of truly knowing God. If your habits this month were the measure, what would they say about whose you are?
Jesus said the first must be the servant of all. Where could you deliberately take the lower place this week for the good of others?

translationNotes.note: I have written to the church renders a phrase the BSB footnote gives literally as I have written something to the church; the reference is likely a short letter now lost, or possibly 2 John. Loves to be first translates philoproteuo, a word found only here.
Malicious slander renders phlyareo with a modifier, literally talking wicked nonsense against; it pictures baseless, empty accusations used as weapons.
Has not seen God echoes John's usage where seeing God means true spiritual knowledge and fellowship, not physical sight; conduct reveals the reality of that relationship.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 3 John 1:9-11. The BSB footnote at verse 9 notes the literal I have written something to the church.
